content: Classical galactosaemia is a rare autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency in the enzyme galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase. This condition can be life-threatening and typically manifests within the first week of life after the initiation of milk feeding. Affected newborns may present with symptoms such as cataracts, severe liver failure, prolonged jaundice, or sepsis caused by Escherichia coli. When galactosaemia is suspected, it is critical to immediately discontinue feeds containing galactose and replace them with a soy-based formula. While most affected infants recover with this intervention, some may not survive. Even with treatment, long-term complications can occur, including cognitive impairments and infertility in females. It has been hypothesized that newborn screening for galactosaemia could enable early detection, thereby preventing severe complications such as acute liver dysfunction and sepsis. This document is an update of a previously published review that aimed to evaluate whether newborn screening for galactosaemia reduces mortality and morbidity, improves clinical outcomes in affected neonates, and enhances the quality of life in older children. To investigate this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register, which includes references from electronic databases, hand-searched journals, and conference abstracts. Additional searches were performed in online trial registries and reference lists of relevant articles. The most recent searches were completed on December 12, 2019, for the Cochrane register and February 2, 2020, for additional resources. The review sought to include randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled clinical studies, whether published or unpublished, that compared newborn screening for galactosaemia with no screening. The goal was to assess differences in outcomes between screened and non-screened populations. However, no eligible studies meeting these criteria were identified. As a result, the review was unable to draw conclusions based on RCTs or controlled clinical studies. Nonetheless, the authors acknowledge the existence of uncontrolled studies that support the effectiveness of newborn screening for galactosaemia. Additionally, several reviews and economic analyses of non-trial literature suggest that implementing screening programs for this condition is appropriate.
